content: It is critical to understand the sequence of events from antiretroviral therapy (ART) enrollment to the treatment of active tuberculosis (TB) disease. This process highlights potential barriers between ART enrollment and TB symptom screening. This is the first of five priority screening cascade indicators for high-burden TB/HIV settings. The numerator is the number of people living with HIV (PLHIV) who were newly initiated on ART and screened for TB during the reporting period. The denominator is the total number of PLHIV newly initiated on ART during the same period. Data for both the numerator and denominator are collected from program records, such as ART registers or electronic medical records (EMRs). Disaggregation is done by gender (male, female, transgender) and age (<15, 15+). The percentage of PLHIV newly initiated on ART who screened positive for TB symptoms is another critical indicator. This measures the proportion of individuals screened for active TB symptoms who tested positive. Routine TB screening among PLHIV, whether newly initiated or already on ART, is essential for identifying presumptive TB cases requiring confirmatory diagnostic testing and determining eligibility for TB preventive therapy (TPT) if active TB is ruled out. Screening positivity rates vary based on TB prevalence and other epidemiological factors. Low positivity rates may indicate inadequate or poor-quality TB screening, especially in high-burden settings. The percentage of PLHIV newly initiated on ART and screened positive for TB symptoms who subsequently undergo TB testing is another key indicator. This measures the proportion of individuals who, after screening positive, receive clinical evaluation and/or appropriate TB diagnostic testing. Proper diagnostic testing is essential for PLHIV who screen positive for TB symptoms. This indicator sheds light on barriers between positive TB symptom screening and diagnostic testing, as per national clinical guidelines. It is the third of five priority screening cascade indicators for high-burden TB/HIV settings. The percentage of PLHIV newly initiated on ART and tested for TB who are diagnosed with active TB disease is another critical measure. This indicator evaluates the proportion of individuals who, after screening positive and undergoing appropriate diagnostic testing, are confirmed to have active TB. Appropriate TB diagnostic testing, based on national or WHO guidelines, is essential for PLHIV who screen positive for TB symptoms. This indicator highlights obstacles between diagnostic testing and TB diagnosis and is the fourth of five priority screening cascade indicators. The percentage of PLHIV newly initiated on ART and diagnosed with active TB who start TB treatment is the final screening cascade indicator. This measures the proportion of individuals who, after being diagnosed with active TB, initiate TB treatment. Prompt initiation of TB treatment and quality clinical monitoring are essential to ensure treatment completion. This indicator identifies gaps between diagnosis and treatment initiation. The percentage of PLHIV on ART who were screened for hepatitis C (HCV) during the reporting period is another important measure. This indicator assesses the coverage of HCV screening among PLHIV on ART. Hepatitis C is a significant co-morbidity in many countries with HIV epidemics. Screening for HCV among PLHIV is crucial for defining disease burden and initiating HCV treatment for eligible patients. The numerator is the number of PLHIV on ART who were screened for HCV (using HCV antibody testing followed by confirmatory testing with HCV RNA or core antigen testing for those HCV Ab-positive) during the reporting period. The denominator is the total number of PLHIV on ART during the same period. Data are collected from program records, and disaggregation is done by gender (male, female, transgender) and age (<15, 15+). The percentage of PLHIV on ART diagnosed with chronic HCV infection who initiated HCV treatment during the reporting period is another critical indicator. This measures the rate of HCV treatment initiation among PLHIV on ART diagnosed with chronic HCV infection. Hepatitis C is a significant co-morbidity in many countries with HIV epidemics. Curative treatment for HCV among PLHIV is essential for reducing morbidity and mortality and achieving HCV elimination. Among PLHIV, people who inject drugs are the most likely to be co-infected with HCV. The numerator is the number of PLHIV on ART diagnosed with chronic viremic HCV infection (defined as positive HCV antibody testing followed by confirmatory testing with HCV RNA or core antigen testing) who initiated HCV treatment during the reporting period. The denominator is the total number of PLHIV on ART diagnosed with chronic viremic HCV infection during the same period. Data are collected from program records, and disaggregation includes people who inject drugs. The estimated number of people living with HIV (PLHIV) is a fundamental measure of the current burden of HIV in a population. This estimate is the basis for program planning and resource needs assessments. It also serves as the denominator for key programmatic indicators and response calculations. The numerator is the estimated number of people infected with HIV who are alive. Mathematical modeling tools, such as Spectrum AIM, generate ageand gender-specific estimates of PLHIV. UNAIDS recommends Spectrum software for these estimates to ensure comparability across countries and incorporate the latest understanding of the HIV epidemic and science. Disaggregation includes gender (male, female, transgender), age (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, 50+), and key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender people, adolescent girls, and young women). The percentage of specific key populations living with HIV is another critical indicator. This measures the severity of the epidemic among key populations and the potential for transmission through bridge populations. In both generalized and concentrated epidemics, key populations typically have higher HIV prevalence than the general population. Stabilizing prevalence among key populations is a measure of the success of the national-level response to HIV. The numerator is the number of people in a specific key population group who test positive for HIV. The denominator is the total number of people in that key population group tested for HIV. Data are collected through probability-based surveys (e.g., BBS) conducted every 3–5 years or annual sentinel surveillance in community or facility settings. Disaggregation includes key populations, gender, age, and duration of engaging in key population-defining behavior. The estimated number of people newly infected with HIV per 1,000 uninfected population is a measure of progress toward ending the HIV/AIDS epidemic and achieving the goal of zero new infections. The overarching goal of the global HIV/AIDS response is to reduce the number of new infections to fewer than 200,000 by 2030. The numerator is the estimated number of people newly infected during the reporting period. The denominator is the total number of uninfected population (or person-years exposed). Mathematical modeling tools, such as Spectrum AIM, incorporate data from geographical and population-specific surveys, surveillance data, and assumptions about HIV transmission. Disaggregation includes gender, age, and key populations. The estimated percentage of children newly infected with HIV from mother-to-child transmission among women living with HIV delivering in the past 12 months measures the impact of interventions to prevent HIV infections in infants. This includes providing pregnant and breastfeeding HIV-positive women with antiretroviral medicines and retaining them on ART through pregnancy and breastfeeding to reduce mother-to-child transmission. The percentage of children living with HIV should decrease as coverage of prevention interventions and the use of more effective ART increase. Countries have increased access to ART and strengthened counseling on infant feeding for HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women.
